units.title: Unit 35 — Crime
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 74–75 (PDF pages 78–79).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe offenders, convictions, sentences and criminal histories without confusing allegations with findings of guilt.
Discuss types of crime, statistics and approaches to prevention using natural lexical combinations.
Use commit, steal and rob with their appropriate objects, and interpret collocations such as crime wave and spate of burglaries.
Recognise differences in register and connotation, including hardened, juvenile and common criminal.

items.pt: criminoso reincidente e experiente; criminoso habitual
items.example: The prosecutor described the suspect as a hardened criminal with several previous convictions.
items.note: Hardened suggests someone experienced in committing offences and unlikely to change easily.

items.pt: cometer uma infração grave; praticar um crime grave
items.example: The fictional defendant was accused of having committed a serious offence.
items.note: Commit is the standard verb with offence and crime, not do an offence.

items.example: She served a sentence for fraud before rebuilding her career.
items.note: Sentence means a court-imposed punishment; serve a sentence often refers to time in prison.

items.example: The organisation called for the release of a political prisoner held for peaceful activism.
items.note: Refers to a person imprisoned for political reasons; the precise classification can be disputed.

items.example: Officials argued that the detainee was a common criminal rather than a political prisoner.
items.note: Common criminal can sound dismissive and contrasts with categories such as political prisoner.

items.example: The security review found that one applicant was a convicted criminal.
items.note: Convicted indicates a finding of guilt by a court, not merely an accusation.

items.example: The records showed a conviction for robbery from several years earlier.
items.note: Conviction for names the offence for which a person was legally found guilty.

items.example: The position required the applicant to disclose any criminal record.
items.note: A criminal record is the official history of a person's criminal convictions or other recorded offences.

items.example: A local programme helps a young offender return to education after release.
items.note: Refers to a young person who has committed an offence; age thresholds depend on the legal system.

items.example: The report described the defendant as a juvenile offender at the time of the incident.
items.note: Juvenile is a formal legal or institutional term relating to people below the relevant adult age.

items.example: He served time in prison and later found stable employment.
items.note: An everyday expression for spending time in prison as punishment; compare serve a sentence.

items.example: The mayor promised additional resources for the fight against crime.
items.note: Fight is figurative here and means organised efforts to reduce criminal activity.

items.example: The police unit was created to target serious crime in the region.
items.note: Target means focus enforcement efforts on a particular kind of offence.

items.example: The study examines how serious crime affects local communities.
items.note: Serious refers to the severity of the offence, not the offender's attitude.

items.pt: criminalidade de rua; crimes cometidos nas ruas
items.example: Residents asked for better lighting to help reduce street crime.
items.note: A broad label for offences such as robbery or assault in public places.

items.example: The neighbourhood reported a rise in vehicle crime during the summer.
items.note: General category covering offences involving vehicles, such as theft or break-ins.

items.pt: invadir uma casa para cometer um crime; arrombar uma residência
items.example: Someone tried to break into a house while its owners were away.
items.note: Break into means enter a building illegally, often by force; it is not the same as break a window.

items.pt: roubar um carro; furtar um carro
items.example: The thieves attempted to steal a car from the car park.
items.note: Steal takes the thing taken as its object; rob normally takes a person, business or place.

items.example: The witness reported that two men tried to rob a person near the station.
items.note: Rob names the victim as object; in ordinary English do not say rob a wallet when you mean steal it.

items.pt: combater a criminalidade; enfrentar o problema do crime
items.example: The new strategy aims to tackle crime through prevention and investigation.
items.note: Tackle means take active steps to deal with a problem; combat crime has a similar meaning.

items.example: Several agencies agreed to work together to combat crime.
items.note: Combat is slightly more formal than tackle or fight in this context.

items.example: The crime rate fell in the fictional district after several changes.
items.note: Rate refers to frequency relative to a population or other measure, not simply the raw number of offences.

items.example: The report says the crime rate comes down when repeat offences are reduced.
items.note: Come down indicates a decrease; use the appropriate tense for a particular reporting period.

items.example: The council funded prevention programmes intended to reduce juvenile crime.
items.note: Juvenile here relates to offences involving people below the legal adult age.

items.example: Community groups and police worked together to fight crime.
items.note: Fight crime is an established figurative expression, not a literal physical fight.

items.example: Local newspapers reported a crime wave after several incidents in one week.
items.note: Refers to a period when many offences occur, often suddenly or unusually frequently.

items.pt: pequenos delitos; criminalidade de menor gravidade
items.example: The project aims to discourage petty crime without overburdening courts.
items.note: Petty means relatively minor; it does not mean that the offence has no consequences.

items.pt: os números da criminalidade; as estatísticas de crimes
items.example: The crime figures need to be interpreted alongside reporting practices.
items.note: Figures are numerical statistics; they may not capture all offences that occurred.

items.pt: uma série de arrombamentos e furtos em residências
items.example: A spate of burglaries prompted residents to improve their door locks.
items.note: A spate is a cluster of unwanted events over a short period, often with of.

items.example: The annual report recorded fewer cases of vehicle theft.
items.note: Theft names the act of stealing; it does not identify who is being robbed.

items.pt: abuso de drogas; uso abusivo de drogas
items.example: The campaign addressed drug abuse and the need for treatment services.
items.note: Abuse here means harmful or excessive use; it is not a synonym for all drug use.

items.pt: um aumento impressionante; um aumento alarmante
items.example: The survey found a staggering increase in reports of attempted fraud.
items.note: Staggering expresses shock at the size of the rise; it is stronger than significant.

items.pt: vandalismo gratuito; vandalismo sem motivo aparente
items.example: Neighbours condemned the mindless vandalism of the public benches.
items.note: Mindless conveys destructive behaviour with no sensible apparent purpose.

items.example: The report explains why some people commit a crime despite the possible penalties.
items.note: The standard verb is commit, not make or do, with crime.

items.pt: cometer uma infração; praticar um delito
items.example: Drivers who commit an offence may receive a penalty notice.
items.note: Offence is common in legal and formal contexts; British spelling is offence.

items.example: Investigators treated the fictional attack as a possible act of terrorism.
items.note: An act of terrorism refers to one instance, not the broader issue of terrorism.

items.pt: uma série de roubos; uma sequência de assaltos
items.example: Police investigated a spate of robberies near the railway station.
items.note: The plural noun names several incidents occurring over a relatively short time.

items.example: The broken public artwork was reported as an act of vandalism.
items.note: An act of vandalism refers to an individual incident of deliberate damage.

items.pt: um escândalo envolvendo abuso de drogas
items.example: The fictional film follows journalists uncovering a drug abuse scandal.
items.note: Scandal refers to publicly criticised misconduct or revelations.

items.word: put police officers on the streets
items.pt: colocar policiais nas ruas; reforçar o policiamento de rua
items.example: The city decided to put more police officers on the streets during busy events.
items.note: A figurative policy phrase for visible deployment, not necessarily literally standing in streets.

items.example: An employee was accused of trying to steal money from the office.
items.note: Steal takes the stolen thing as object; compare rob a bank or rob a person.

items.example: The characters planned to rob a bank in the opening scene of the film.
items.note: Rob takes the institution as object, while steal takes the money or property.

units.title: Unit 36 — News
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 76–77 (PDF pages 80–81).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Describe how news appears and spreads using expressions such as break, leak out and hit the headlines.
Distinguish major headlines from individual news items, and use the uncountable noun news correctly.
Report public announcements, official talks, campaigns and developing events with established collocations.
Describe sudden developments and incidents, including loss of control, captivity, fires and failed talks.

items.pt: uma notícia vem a público; uma notícia estoura
items.example: When a news story breaks, editors may have only a few confirmed details.
items.note: Break describes the first public emergence of a story, not physical damage.

items.example: More news comes in as reporters contact witnesses.
items.note: Come in means arrive or be received, particularly in news broadcasting.

items.pt: uma informação sigilosa vaza; notícias vazam
items.example: News leaks out when confidential details reach journalists without official approval.
items.note: Leak suggests information becoming public despite an intention to keep it secret.

items.pt: virar manchete; ganhar destaque na imprensa
items.example: The discovery could hit the headlines when the results are published.
items.note: Hit the headlines means become prominent news, often suddenly.

items.pt: virar manchete; ganhar repercussão na mídia
items.example: The athlete's unexpected retirement made headlines across the country.
items.note: Make headlines means attract notable press attention, not physically write a heading.

items.example: The election result became a front-page headline the next morning.
items.note: Front-page indicates placement on the first page of a newspaper.

items.pt: as últimas notícias; as notícias mais recentes
items.example: We checked the latest news before leaving for the airport.
items.note: Use latest for most recent information; last news is not the usual expression.

items.example: The court's decision became headline news across the country.
items.note: Used for a major story; contrast with an incidental item of news.

items.pt: notícia de primeira página; notícia de grande destaque
items.example: The scientific breakthrough was front-page news in several newspapers.
items.note: Refers to news important enough to receive prominent newspaper coverage.

items.pt: uma notícia; um item do noticiário
items.example: The presenter introduced an item of news about a new railway line.
items.note: News is uncountable; say an item or a piece of news rather than a news.

items.pt: publicar uma reportagem; veicular uma notícia
items.example: The local paper decided to run a story about the community laboratory.
items.note: Run a story means publish or broadcast it; not the same as the story breaking.

items.example: She flicked through the newspaper while waiting for her train.
items.note: Flick through means look quickly at pages without reading everything closely.

items.example: The minister will hold a news conference after the committee meeting.
items.note: A news conference is a meeting at which officials address journalists and answer questions.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: In a surprising turn of events, the two organisations announced an agreement.
items.note: A turn of events describes an unexpected change in how a situation develops.

items.pt: dar sinal verde aos planos; autorizar os planos
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The council gave the go-ahead to plans for a new science centre.
items.note: Give the go-ahead means grant permission for a proposed activity or project.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The organisers invited all interested parties to the public consultation.
items.note: Interested parties are people or groups with a stake in an issue, not merely curious people.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The two companies agreed to hold talks about future cooperation.
items.note: Usually refers to organised discussions between groups, often about a serious issue.

items.pt: apresentar as linhas gerais de um plano
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The director outlined plans for upgrading the laboratory.
items.note: Outline means describe the main elements without every detail.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The charity launched a campaign to encourage safer cycling.
items.note: Launch is a natural verb for starting a public initiative or organised effort.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The documentary examines a national anti-smoking campaign from the 1990s.
items.note: Anti-smoking modifies campaign; the hyphen helps identify its purpose.

items.pt: deixar um cargo de alto nível; renunciar a um cargo de destaque
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The executive resigned from a top job after several years in leadership.
items.note: Resign describes voluntarily leaving a position; top job means a senior role.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The unusual announcement quickly attracted attention from journalists.
items.note: Attention can be positive, negative or simply increased public notice.

items.pt: uma decisão controversa; uma decisão polêmica
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The board faced criticism over a controversial decision about ticket prices.
items.note: Controversial means provoking disagreement, not necessarily unlawful.

items.pt: voltar a cobrar taxas; reintroduzir cobranças
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The museum decided to re-introduce charges for special exhibitions.
items.note: Here charges are fees; re-introduce means bring them back after a period without them.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: In the fictional drama, an aid worker was taken hostage during the conflict.
items.note: Taken hostage means held to pressure another party, not merely detained.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: In the novel, rebel forces seize control of the fictional city's airport.
items.note: Seize emphasises taking control suddenly or by force.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The organisation feared it might lose control of its operations during the dispute.
items.note: A broad phrase for no longer exercising authority over a place or process.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: Scientists kept a close watch on the volcano as activity increased.
items.note: Keep a close watch on means monitor carefully and continuously for changes.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: We will keep everyone informed as the investigation progresses.
items.note: The person receiving updates comes between keep and informed; the phrase can be personalised in examples.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The station promised further updates as the news develops.
items.note: Describes a story changing or acquiring new information over time.

items.pt: negociações de paz fracassam; conversações de paz são interrompidas
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: In the fictional account, peace talks break down after the delegates leave.
items.note: Break down means fail to continue successfully; contrast with simply ending a meeting.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The novel describes a family displaced by a civil war.
items.note: Refers to armed conflict between groups within the same country.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: Lightning struck a building on the edge of town during the storm.
items.note: Strike is the natural verb for lightning making contact with something; forms include struck.

items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: The old electrical panel caught fire after a component failed.
items.note: Catch fire means begin burning, not merely be close to flames.

items.pt: nenhuma perda de vidas; sem vítimas fatais
items.section: B · The language of news stories
items.example: Firefighters confirmed there had been no loss of life after the incident.
items.note: Formal news-reporting expression meaning nobody died, even if damage occurred.

items.example: In an unexpected turn of events, the organisers cancelled the vote.
items.note: Unexpected and surprising can both modify turn of events, with similar meanings.

items.pt: manter a população informada; manter o público informado
items.example: The agency promised to keep the public informed about the repairs.
items.note: A concrete version of keep someone informed, often used in official announcements.

items.example: In the historical novel, several soldiers were taken captive after the battle.
items.note: Captive refers to imprisonment or capture; hostage adds the idea of leverage or demands.

items.pt: um raio cai; raios atingem algo
items.example: When lightning strikes, nearby buildings can suffer damage.
items.note: Lightning is the subject of strike; struck is the past tense.

items.example: The operations team maintained a close watch on network traffic.
items.note: A close watch is careful monitoring; keep a close watch on is a common full expression.

items.example: The organisation held a press conference to clarify the announcement.
items.note: Press conference is a widely used alternative to news conference in journalistic settings.
